name: Corporate Finance & Valuation
title: Valuation Analyst
blurb: Valuing companies and projects is the shared language of strategy consulting cases, SAP FI/CO controlling work and the trading desks that Murex and Calypso serve.

chapters.title: Time value of money
chapters.read: A corporate finance textbook's opening chapters on compounding, discounting, annuities and perpetuities; practise each formula alongside Excel's FV, PV and PMT functions.
chapters.produce: Build an Excel sheet that computes FV, PV, annuity PV and a loan payment for any rate and term, and check it by hand against 5 worked cases.

quiz.q: You deposit ¥100,000 at 5% per year, compounded annually. What is it worth after 3 years? (round to the nearest yen)
What is the present value of ¥1,000,000 received in 4 years if the discount rate is 6% per year? (nearest yen)
What is the present value of ¥100,000 received at the end of each year for 5 years at 4%? (nearest yen)
A perpetuity pays C per year forever, with the first payment one year from now. At discount rate r, its present value is:
opts: C × r
C / r
quiz.ex: The PV of a level perpetuity starting in one year is C divided by r.

quiz.q: Using the rule of 72, roughly how long does money take to double at 8% per year?
opts: About 9 years
About 4 years
About 6 years
About 12 years
quiz.ex: 72 / 8 = 9 years (exact answer: about 9.0 years).

quiz.q: Which change increases the present value of a fixed future cash flow?
opts: The discount rate rises
The cash flow arrives later
The nominal rate stays the same but compounding becomes more frequent
The discount rate falls
quiz.ex: A lower discount rate shrinks the denominator (1 + r)^t, so PV rises. The other changes all reduce PV.

chapters.title: NPV, IRR and payback
chapters.read: The capital budgeting chapter of a corporate finance textbook: NPV, IRR, payback and why NPV is the preferred rule; practise with Excel's NPV and IRR functions.
chapters.produce: Evaluate three hypothetical projects for a Yamanashi winery (NPV, IRR, payback) in one spreadsheet and write a one-paragraph recommendation.

quiz.q: A project costs ¥1,000m today and returns ¥400m at the end of each of the next 3 years. At a 10% cost of capital, what is its NPV in ¥m? (2 decimals)
You invest ¥1,000,000 today and receive ¥1,210,000 in two years, with nothing in between. What is the IRR in %?
A project costs ¥500 and generates ¥150, ¥200, ¥250 and ¥300 in years 1–4 (spread evenly within each year). What is its payback period in years?
quiz.ex: After year 2: 150 + 200 = 350 recovered; 150 still needed out of year 3's 250 = 0.6 of a year. Payback = 2.6 years.

quiz.q: For independent projects, which is the correct NPV decision rule?
opts: Accept projects whose IRR is below the cost of capital
Accept projects with NPV above zero at the cost of capital
Accept the shortest-payback project regardless of NPV
Accept any project whose undiscounted inflows exceed the investment
quiz.ex: A positive NPV means the project earns more than the cost of capital and adds value.

quiz.q: What is the main weakness of the simple payback method?
opts: It needs an estimate of the cost of capital
It ignores cash flows after the payback date
It always rejects positive-NPV projects
It cannot handle uneven cash flows
quiz.ex: Payback stops counting once the investment is recovered, so it ignores later cash flows. Simple payback also ignores the time value of money.

quiz.q: Two mutually exclusive projects differ greatly in size. Project A has the higher IRR, and Project B has the higher NPV. Which should you choose, and why?
opts: Project A, because a higher IRR always means more value
Either one, because IRR and NPV always rank projects the same way
Neither, because IRR cannot be used when projects are of different sizes
Project B, because NPV measures the value added in yen and IRR can rank projects of different sizes wrongly
quiz.ex: For mutually exclusive projects, choose the higher NPV. IRR is a percentage and ignores scale.

chapters.title: Cost of capital: CAPM and WACC
chapters.read: A corporate finance textbook's chapters on risk and return, beta, CAPM and the weighted average cost of capital, including the tax shield on debt and market-value weights.
chapters.produce: Estimate the WACC of one listed Japanese company: take its beta, an assumed risk-free rate and market premium, and its market cap and debt, and document every input.

quiz.q: A stock has a beta of 0.8. The risk-free rate is 0.5% and the expected market return is 6.5%. What is its cost of equity under CAPM, in %?
Equity is worth ¥600bn and debt ¥400bn (market values). The cost of equity is 8%, the pre-tax cost of debt is 2% and the tax rate is 30%. What is the WACC in %?
A company borrows at 3% before tax, and its tax rate is 30%. What is its after-tax cost of debt in %?
In CAPM, beta measures:
opts: How sensitive the stock's returns are to market returns (systematic risk)
The total volatility of the stock's returns
The company's debt-to-equity ratio
The dividend yield relative to the market
quiz.ex: Beta captures only market-related (systematic) risk, which diversification cannot remove.

quiz.q: Why is the cost of debt multiplied by (1 − tax rate) in WACC?
opts: Lenders pay the company's tax on the interest
Dividends are tax-deductible but interest is not
Interest is tax-deductible, so the tax shield lowers the effective cost of debt
Regulators cap interest rates at the after-tax level
quiz.ex: Interest expense reduces taxable income, so each yen of interest costs the company only (1 − t) yen after tax.

quiz.q: Which weights should WACC use?
opts: Book value of total assets
The number of shareholders versus the number of lenders
Market values of debt and equity (ideally the target capital structure)
Revenue split by business segment
quiz.ex: WACC reflects what investors require today, so it weights capital by market (or target) values.

chapters.title: Free cash flow and building a DCF
chapters.read: A valuation textbook or investment-banking training guide's chapters on unlevered free cash flow, forecasting revenue, margins, capex and working capital, and the bridge from enterprise value to equity value.
chapters.produce: Build a 5-year DCF for a simple listed company in Excel: revenue drivers, UFCF, discounting at WACC and an EV-to-equity bridge ending in a value per share.

quiz.q: EBIT is ¥1,000m, the tax rate is 30%, D&A is ¥200m, capex is ¥300m and net working capital rises by ¥50m. What is unlevered free cash flow in ¥m?
quiz.ex: UFCF = EBIT × (1 − t) + D&A − capex − ΔNWC = 700 + 200 − 300 − 50 = 550.

quiz.q: Forecast FCF is ¥100m, ¥110m and ¥121m in years 1–3 and WACC is 10%. What is the PV of these three cash flows in ¥m? (2 decimals)
Enterprise value is ¥5,000m, debt is ¥1,500m, cash is ¥300m and there are 20m shares. What is the equity value per share in ¥?
Unlevered free cash flow should be discounted at:
opts: WACC
The cost of equity only
The risk-free rate
The after-tax cost of debt
quiz.ex: UFCF belongs to all capital providers (debt and equity), so the matching rate is WACC, and the result is enterprise value.

quiz.q: What does an increase in net working capital do to free cash flow?
opts: Increases it
Nothing, because it is only a balance-sheet item
It affects net income but not cash flow
Reduces it, because cash is tied up in receivables and inventory
quiz.ex: Growing receivables and inventory use cash, so ΔNWC is subtracted.

quiz.q: Why is depreciation and amortisation added back when computing FCF from EBIT?
opts: It is cash received from selling old assets
It is a non-cash expense that was deducted to arrive at EBIT
Tax law requires it to be paid in cash later
It represents next year's capex
quiz.ex: D&A reduces EBIT without any cash leaving the company. The cash outflow is captured by capex.

chapters.title: Terminal value and sensitivity
chapters.read: A valuation textbook's chapter on terminal value (Gordon growth versus exit multiple), discounting it correctly and building sensitivity tables with Excel data tables.
chapters.produce: Add both terminal value methods to your DCF and a 5×5 WACC-versus-growth sensitivity table, then write three sentences on what drives the value.

quiz.q: Year-5 FCF is ¥100m, long-term growth is 2% and WACC is 8%. What is the Gordon growth terminal value at the end of year 5, in ¥m?
Discount that terminal value of ¥1,700m (at the end of year 5) to today at 8%. What is its PV in ¥m?
A target's year-5 EBITDA is ¥80m and comparable companies trade at 8.0x EV/EBITDA. What is the exit-multiple terminal value in ¥m?
quiz.ex: 80 × 8.0 = 640 (value at the end of year 5, before discounting).

quiz.q: Why must WACC be greater than the growth rate g in the Gordon growth formula?
opts: Because tax rules cap g at WACC
Because FCF × (1 + g) / (WACC − g) explodes or turns negative when g ≥ WACC
Because g is always measured in real terms and WACC in nominal terms
It does not matter; the formula works for any g
quiz.ex: The perpetuity formula only converges when the discount rate exceeds the growth rate.

quiz.q: The two inputs most often put on the axes of a DCF sensitivity table are:
opts: Share price and number of employees
Tax rate and audit fees
Dividend per share and the share count
WACC and the terminal growth rate (or exit multiple)
quiz.ex: Terminal value is usually most of EV, and it is driven by WACC and g (or the exit multiple).

quiz.q: Holding WACC constant, what happens to enterprise value when the terminal growth rate rises?
opts: It increases
It decreases
It does not change, because TV is discounted
Only equity value changes, not EV
quiz.ex: A higher g raises the terminal value and therefore EV.

chapters.title: Trading and transaction comparables
chapters.read: A valuation textbook's chapter on relative valuation: choosing peers, calculating EV and equity value, EV/EBITDA, P/E and EV/sales, and how precedent-transaction multiples differ.
chapters.produce: Build a comps table for 5 Japanese listed peers in one sector (EV, EBITDA, EPS, multiples, median), and value a sixth company from the median.

quiz.q: Peers trade at a median EV/EBITDA of 9.0x. The target's EBITDA is ¥50bn and its net debt is ¥100bn. What is the implied equity value in ¥bn?
A company's EPS is ¥120 and peers trade at a P/E of 15x. What is the implied share price in ¥?
Market cap is ¥800bn, debt ¥300bn, cash ¥150bn and non-controlling interests ¥50bn. What is enterprise value in ¥bn?
Why is EV/EBITDA often preferred to P/E for comparing companies with different debt levels?
opts: P/E cannot be calculated for profitable companies
EV/EBITDA includes interest expense in the denominator
EV and EBITDA are both measured before financing, so the multiple is largely unaffected by capital structure
P/E ignores the share price
quiz.ex: Net income and the share price are both affected by leverage; EV/EBITDA looks at the whole firm before interest.

quiz.q: Compared with trading comparables, precedent transaction multiples are usually:
opts: Lower, because buyers always negotiate discounts
Identical, because both use current share prices
Higher, because buyers pay a control premium
Unrelated to valuation
quiz.ex: Acquirers pay for control and synergies, so deal multiples typically exceed trading multiples.

quiz.q: Which multiple mixes an enterprise-level numerator with an equity-level denominator, making it inconsistent?
opts: EV / net income
EV / EBITDA
Price / EPS
EV / sales
quiz.ex: Net income is after interest and belongs to shareholders only, so it should be paired with equity value (P/E), not EV.

chapters.title: Reading 決算短信 and 有価証券報告書
chapters.read: Download one company's 決算短信 (from its IR page or TDnet) and its 有価証券報告書 (from EDINET), and map the Japanese P&L lines (売上高 to 当期純利益), the balance sheet, the cash flow statement and the segment notes to their English equivalents.
chapters.produce: Make a bilingual one-page cheat sheet of 30 key line items and section names, then extract 5 years of 売上高, 営業利益 and 営業CF for one company into a spreadsheet.

quiz.q: 売上高 is ¥10,000m, 売上原価 is ¥6,500m and 販売費及び一般管理費 is ¥2,800m. What is the operating margin (営業利益 / 売上高) in %?
営業利益 is ¥500m, 営業外収益 is ¥40m and 営業外費用 is ¥60m. What is 経常利益 in ¥m?
quiz.ex: 経常利益 = 営業利益 + 営業外収益 − 営業外費用 = 500 + 40 − 60 = 480.

quiz.q: Where would you normally first find a listed Japanese company's own forecast for next year's 売上高 and 営業利益?
opts: The audit report in 有価証券報告書
The company's commercial registry (登記簿)
The shareholder register (株主名簿)
決算短信 (the summary earnings release)
quiz.ex: 決算短信 is published soon after the period ends and usually includes the company's 業績予想 (earnings forecast).

quiz.q: 有価証券報告書 is filed under which law, and through which system?
opts: The Companies Act only, via TDnet
The Financial Instruments and Exchange Act (金融商品取引法), via EDINET
The Corporation Tax Act, via e-Tax
Stock exchange rules only, via the exchange website
quiz.ex: The 有価証券報告書 is a statutory disclosure under the FIEA, filed on EDINET. 決算短信 is a stock exchange disclosure published on TDnet.

quiz.q: 経常利益 differs from 営業利益 mainly because it also includes:
opts: Extraordinary gains and losses, such as gains on asset sales
Non-operating income and expenses, such as interest and dividends received or paid
Income taxes
Cost of sales
quiz.ex: Extraordinary items (特別利益・特別損失) come after 経常利益, and taxes come after that.

quiz.q: Which section of 有価証券報告書 sets out the main risks management sees in the business?
opts: 大株主の状況
連結貸借対照表
監査報告書
事業等のリスク
quiz.ex: 事業等のリスク (business risks) is the narrative risk section. The others are the major shareholders, the balance sheet and the audit report.

chapters.title: M&A basics: synergies, accretion and dilution
chapters.read: An M&A or investment-banking textbook's chapters on deal rationale, control premiums, valuing synergies, goodwill, and building an accretion/dilution analysis for stock and cash deals.
chapters.produce: Build a one-sheet accretion/dilution model for a hypothetical all-stock acquisition between two Japanese companies, with a toggle for synergies.

quiz.q: The acquirer has net income of ¥1,000m and 100m shares. It buys a target with net income of ¥200m by issuing 25m new shares. Ignoring synergies and costs, what is the pro forma EPS in ¥?
quiz.ex: (1,000 + 200) / (100 + 25) = 1,200 / 125 = ¥9.6, compared with ¥10.0 before, so the deal is dilutive.

quiz.q: A deal brings after-tax cost synergies of ¥30m per year forever, valued at 10%, and one-off integration costs of ¥50m today. What is the net present value of the synergies in ¥m?
A target's undisturbed share price is ¥1,000, and the bidder offers ¥1,300 per share. What is the control premium in %?
Which type of synergy do analysts usually treat as more certain?
opts: Cost synergies
Revenue synergies
Both are always equally certain
Synergies from a higher share price
quiz.ex: Cost savings, such as closing duplicate offices, are more under management's control than extra sales.

quiz.q: Ignoring synergies and fees, when is an all-stock acquisition accretive to the acquirer's EPS?
opts: When the acquirer's P/E is lower than the P/E paid for the target
Whenever the target has more employees
When the acquirer's P/E is higher than the P/E paid for the target
Always, because issuing shares never dilutes EPS
quiz.ex: A high-P/E acquirer issues relatively few shares for each yen of earnings it buys.

quiz.q: Goodwill arises in an acquisition when:
opts: The target's book value exceeds the purchase price
The acquirer pays in cash rather than shares
The purchase price exceeds the fair value of the target's identifiable net assets
The target has no debt
quiz.ex: Goodwill is the excess of the price paid over the fair value of the identifiable net assets acquired.

boss.q: You borrow ¥10,000,000 for 5 years at 3% per year, repaid in equal annual payments at each year-end. What is the annual payment? (nearest yen)
A loan quotes 12% per year compounded monthly. What is the effective annual rate in %? (2 decimals)
An unlevered (asset) beta is 0.8. The target D/E is 0.5 and the tax rate is 30%. Using βL = βU × (1 + (1 − t) × D/E), what is the levered beta?
FCF is ¥100m in year 1 and ¥105m in year 2. After that FCF grows at 2% forever, and WACC is 9%. What is enterprise value today in ¥m? (2 decimals)
A target's EBITDA is ¥40bn, peers trade at 7.5x EV/EBITDA, net debt is ¥60bn and there are 12m shares. What is the implied value per share in ¥?
A project costs ¥1,000 today. It generates FCF of ¥80 in year 1, growing at 1% per year forever, and WACC is 7%. What is its NPV? (2 decimals)
You need audited consolidated financial statements with full notes, segment information and the business-risk section for a Japanese listed company. Which document is best?
opts: 有価証券報告書
決算短信's summary page only
The company's press release on a new product
The 株主総会招集通知 cover letter
boss.ex: The 有価証券報告書 is the full statutory annual report, with audited statements and detailed notes.

boss.q: In a DCF, terminal value makes up 80% of enterprise value. What does this mainly imply?
opts: The explicit forecast years do not need checking at all
The company must be overvalued
WACC no longer affects the result
The valuation is highly sensitive to the WACC and long-term growth (or exit multiple) assumptions
boss.ex: When most of the value sits in the terminal value, small changes in WACC or g move EV a lot, so sensitivity tables matter.

boss.q: Which pairing of cash flow, discount rate and result is consistent?
opts: Unlevered FCF discounted at the cost of equity gives equity value directly
Unlevered FCF discounted at WACC gives enterprise value
Levered FCF discounted at WACC gives enterprise value
Net income discounted at the risk-free rate gives enterprise value
boss.ex: Cash flows to all capital providers match WACC and give EV. Cash flows to equity match the cost of equity and give equity value.

boss.q: An acquirer pays all cash, funded by debt with an after-tax cost of 2%, for a target priced at a P/E of 20 (an earnings yield of 5%). Ignoring synergies and fees, the deal is most likely:
opts: Dilutive, because a P/E of 20 is always too high
Accretive, because the 2% after-tax cost of debt is below the target's 5% earnings yield
Neutral, because cash deals never change EPS
Dilutive, because adding debt always lowers EPS
boss.ex: The target earns 5% on the price paid, while the funding costs 2% after tax, so EPS rises.
